column5: Rodney's preface states his position openly: written 1972 in Dar es Salaam (Tanzania); 'African development is possible only on the basis of a radical break with the international capitalist system'; says it aims at Africans 'to explore further the nature of their exploitation', not at academic standards; final section by A. M. Babu (Tanzanian minister) on strategy. So the book is a self-declared political-economy argument (dependency school), to be presented as one position beside Moyo and mainstream development economics

Introduction (1981, Harding/Strickland/Hill) is partisan biography: Rodney b. 13/03/1942 Georgetown, first-class history UCWI 1963, SOAS PhD (Upper Guinea Coast 1545-1800), taught Dar es Salaam 1966-67 and 1969-72, expelled from Jamaica 10/1968, Guyana 1974 (WPA), killed by a bomb 13/06/1980; the editors say it was the result of Burnham's regime (an accusation; Guyana's later 2016 commission of inquiry concluded the state was responsible [check current]). Book published 1972 (Bogle-L'Ouverture/Tanzania Publishing House); Howard University Press US edition 1974; ends analysis around the 1950s-60s. Quoted thesis: 'imperialist system bears major responsibility for African economic retardation by draining African wealth' at one level, and 'African accomplices' at another; 'every African has a responsibility to understand the system and work for its overthrow'. Useful to show Rodney explicitly sees African agency and complicity (not only victimhood)

Rodney's framework (ch.1): development = growing capacity to deal with the environment (science, technology, work organisation) in a Marxist stage model (communalism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, socialism); every continent developed independently; uneven development; superstructure (beliefs, institutions) explains different rates (China example). He presents capitalism as now an outmoded brake that must be overthrown, and writes that 'the advance of socialism over the last fifty-odd years' shows capitalism 'rapidly expiring' (a 1972 prediction that history overtook: USSR dissolved 1991; Tanzania's ujamaa model he praised failed economically). Flag as a dated, ideological premise; stage-model is contested among historians of Africa

Rodney's key definition (the claim the course must label as a position): underdevelopment is not absence of development but 'a particular relationship of exploitation: the exploitation of one country by another'; 'African and Asian societies were developing independently until they were taken over'; export of surplus drained resources and labour. 1968 UN per-capita income table he gives: USA $3,578, Canada $2,247, France $1,738, UK $1,560; Africa overall $140 (1965); South Africa $543, Zambia $225, Ghana $198, Kenya $107, Tanzania $62, Congo $52, Malawi $52. Arithmetic check: US/Africa = 25.6x; US/Congo = 68.8x; dated nominal dollars, not PPP, 1960s, not comparable with modern data. Also trade share of 'underdeveloped countries' fell from ~30 per cent (1938) to under 20 per cent (1960s). Use as the book's baseline, labelled 1960s data

Rodney also criticises African elites inside this definition: 'principal industry of many underdeveloped countries is administration' (60 per cent of Dahomey's internal revenue on salaries; Gabon one MP per 6,000 people vs one per 100,000 in France), claims civil servants and politicians squander wealth on 'cars, whisky and perfume' and that 'brain drain' and costly foreign experts are structural problems. So Rodney is not only blaming Europe: he assigns the African political class responsibility (consistent with his Introduction). Good counterweight to a caricature that his thesis is purely external. Also cites UN: Africa 9 per cent of world population but 28 per cent of world mineral production value (UN Survey of Economic Conditions in Africa to 1964) -- dated

Rodney's causal argument made explicit (the position the course must present as one of two): (a) underdevelopment has external causes: unequal exchange (metropoles set prices of exports and imports and freight), foreign ownership of land, mines, banks, (b) loan repayment on official loans in underdeveloped countries rose from $400m to ~$700m a year in the 1960s and over $500m flowed outward from them in 1965 (his figures, 1960s, he says likely underestimates), (c) 'structural dependence' (metropole-satellite), culture, church, language, aid as a 'subtle' form, (d) local 'sell-outs' and coups as symptoms. He attacks the idea that lack of skills is a cause (calls it a symptom). Counter-evidence to weigh: Moyo/Bauer argue the reverse (aid and state-led policy cause it); specialists on Africa dispute single-cause 'exploitation' explanations and the later East Asian development case sits uneasily with dependency theory; add note that the dependency school's central prediction (break with capitalism = development) was not borne out by the socialist-aligned African experiments of the 1970s [contested]. Rodney's claim that 'socialist countries never owned any part of Africa... are not involved in robbery' is a 1972 assertion not supported by later Soviet-bloc arms/loan history [dated, contested]

Rodney on the 'balance sheet' of colonialism (ch.VI, answers the 'colonialism brought railways and hospitals' view): argues services were tiny and aimed at export extraction. Specific figures he gives (1930s unless stated): social-service spending per head 1934 UK GBP 6 15s vs Ghana 7s 4d, Nigeria and Nyasaland under 1s 9d; Algeria infant mortality 39 per 1,000 (settlers) vs 170 (urban Algerians); Ibadan 11 hospital beds for ~50 Europeans vs 34 for half a million Africans; Nigeria 12 modern hospitals for 4,000 Europeans vs 52 for 40 million Africans; South Africa TB commission 1912; Embakasi airport built from 1953 using Mau Mau detainees; Credit to Natives (Restriction) Ordinance 1931. Roads and railways 'all led down to the sea'; colonial currency boards held African reserves in London/Paris. A comparison for Module 1 'forms of rule' and Module 5 context. Rodney's case rests on selected figures; economic historians (e.g. Austin, Frankema, Hopkins) argue colonial investment varied, so label as one side of a historiographical debate [CONTESTED]

Rodney on colonial 'development funds' and deindustrialisation: CD&W grants 1946-56 under 1 per cent to industry, FIDES 1949-53 under 0.5 per cent; Nigeria's Ten Year Plan voted GBP 1.824m for agriculture out of GBP 53m; funds tied to metropolitan goods; Senegal groundnut-oil mills (1927) restricted after French protest; Africans barred from owning cotton gins (Uganda); no 'backward and forward linkages' (Guinea bauxite example); Chunya gold exhausted 1933-53; African cash-crop income rarely over GBP 10 a year; Chad cotton: fifty days' work to buy three metres of cloth. Figures are his and mostly from 1930s-50s colonial reports; Module 1 'forms of rule' could cite the point that colonial economies were organised for export, with the debate on whether colonial rule also left usable infrastructure noted as contested. Also his claim that the African nation-state was colonial; he accepts later nationalism adopted colonial borders (consistent with the OAU 1964 border decision, Module 4)

Rodney on ethnicity and Biafra (direct bearing on Module 6 Biafra lesson): argues the Nigerian civil war was not an age-old 'tribal' conflict; says nowhere in pre-colonial Nigeria is there a massacre of Igbo by Hausa, and 'tribalism' was a product of colonial administration, regional separation (Nigeria), the Mailo land settlement 1900 and 'sub-imperialist' Baganda (Uganda), and the 1934 Kenya commission on racial/tribal blocks; Belgian and South African divide-and-rule (Bantustan 'Zulu/Xhosa/Sotho' development). Also mocks the view that the war was tribal by saying that would make Shell and Gulf Oil 'tribes' (an oil-interest argument). Verify against Welsh/Module 5 (Bantustan policy is supported by Welsh) and against standard Biafra histories (the 1966 anti-Igbo pogroms in northern Nigeria are well documented, so his 'no massacre' claim concerns pre-colonial times only). Present as the 'colonial construction' view (shared with Ranger/Mamdani), which specialists qualify: pre-colonial identities existed but were hardened by colonial rule [CONTESTED/refined]

Rodney on agency and the colonial state: colonialism 'removed Africans from history' (Memmi, Fanon, Cabral), warrant chiefs invented in Igboland, puppet rulers; says Africans' initiative was mere response to colonial options, until the 1960s; women's status declined (loss of Queen Mother/Rain-Queen type roles; men migrate and women carry farm work); roads led to ports; Gold Coast to Ivory Coast phone calls routed via London and Paris; only ~10 per cent of Africa's trade was internal late in the colonial period (compare Moyo's ~10 per cent intra-African exports in 2008: the figure is similar across 50 years, which supports a structural reading). Contrasts with the 'sympathetic school' (African initiative) he rejects: the course can present this historiographical split (Rodney vs the agency school) in Module 1/4

Rodney on monoculture and 'growth without development' (Module 4/6 link to post-colonial export dependence): Senegal and Gambia groundnuts 85-90 per cent of money earnings; Liberia rubber, Gold Coast cocoa, Sudan cotton, Tanganyika sisal; Gambia rice displaced by groundnuts; cocoa swollen-shoot disease 1940s. His claim 'Monoculture was a colonialist invention' is strong; many economic historians say export specialisation also followed African farmers' own responses to world prices, while the colonial state pushed taxes and infrastructure towards it [CONTESTED/refined]. Useful for tying Module 1 (colonial economies) to Module 6 (commodity dependence and structural adjustment)

Rodney's nutrition claims (1972) need caution before use: he argues colonialism caused 'stunting' and chronic malnutrition, citing Josue de Castro, tooth-decay observations in Kenya, kwashiorkor, pellagra, scurvy in Tanganyika gold fields; some of these are well-evidenced local cases (e.g. mine-compound scurvy, maize-meal diets and pellagra), but 'pre-colonial Africans showed no clinical deficiency' and Maasai/Tutsi 'superb physique' claims are generalisations that modern nutrition and demographic history do not support (famines, disease and high infant mortality existed before 1885). Do not teach as fact; if used, cite as Rodney's argument. Also: his admission that modern medicine and immunisation were 'objectively positive' though limited

Education data (supports Module 4 'inheritance at independence' and Hochschild's Congo-at-independence point): Rodney gives Congo at independence with only 16 graduates out of 13 million+ (Hochschild says fewer than thirty African university graduates in the whole territory: the two figures are the same order, 16 vs 'fewer than thirty'; reconcile by citing both with their definitions [FIRM that it was tiny, exact count PROBABLE range 16-30]); education's share of revenue 1935: French West Africa 4.03 per cent, Nigeria 3.4 per cent, Kenya 2.26 per cent (1946); French Equatorial Africa 22,000 pupils 1938, FWA 77,000 in 1938; Uganda 1959 spend per pupil GBP 11 African, 38 Indian, 186 European; Senegal's Dakar lycee 1946 723 pupils, 174 African; Southern Rhodesia 1958 pyramid: 227,000 kindergarten, 77,000 to grade 1, 10,000 to grade 6, 3,000 secondary, 13 reached grade 12; UNESCO: illiteracy 80-85 per cent, 3 in 100 see a secondary school, under 2 per thousand higher education (c.1960s). Assimilado/assimile/evolue systems named. Rodney's quote 'education for underdevelopment'; counter-view: missions did build much African schooling and African demand for schooling drove expansion [refined]. Dated data

Date error in Rodney: he says John Chilembwe 'led an armed nationalist uprising in Nyasaland (Malawi) in 1917'; the Chilembwe rising took place in January 1915 [check; widely given as 23/01/1915]. Use 1915 and cite Rodney only for the point about independent churches as a vehicle of protest. Also: Bantu Education Act 1953 (matches Welsh), Rodney reads it as divide-and-rule between Zulu/Sotho/Xhosa/Venda; French/Portuguese assimilation policies (assimile, assimilado, evolue) with Portugal's own near-50 per cent illiteracy in 1960 as irony

Rodney on missions and education as ideology (Module 1 forms of rule / Module 3 Pan-Africanism): missionaries as agents of colonialism ('each mission station is an exercise in colonisation', Sir Harry Johnston), churches teaching docility, independent African churches as protest (Chilembwe), the mission-educated elite as alienated 'black Scotsmen'; Blaise Diagne quoted as always 'European'; Belgian vernacular-language policy as division; French policy of spreading French as 'national defence' (Etienne 1880s; Alliance Francaise 1884); Gov. Cameron of Tanganyika wanting 'fair-minded Englishmen'. His own concessions: missionaries opposed twin-killing and trial by ordeal, and Schweitzer's hospital is attacked (a sharp, contested critique). Mission-educated Africans were also the leaders of nationalist movements (Nkrumah, Mandela, Banda); the course can note that irony [refined]

Rodney's neo-colonialism thesis for independence (Module 4): colonial education produced 'cadres' (French: Ponty, Sarraut, Brevie quotes; Alliance Francaise) and at independence the powers 'turned to colonial cadres' and handed over; armies (King's African Rifles, Force Publique) produced the sergeants who became generals; named elite schools (Gordon College, Alliance High, Budo, Tabora, Mfantsipim, William Ponty, Makerere, Achimota). He says the changeover 'did have the element of conspiracy in it' but also insists independence was won by Africans, not given. Strong claim; contested by historians who stress African nationalist agency and the speed of the 1957-64 transfers. Note his explicit statement 'the choice that Africa should be free was not made by the colonial powers but by the people of Africa'

Rodney's 'development by contradiction': 'the only positive development in colonialism was when it ended'; Africans' own initiative in schooling (villages building and paying for schools; Igbo palm-oil income funding schools; 1930 FWA governor-general reports 'clamouring'; Somalia's first secondary school 1949 by a Somali trader; Kikuyu Independent Schools Association 1929; Beecher report 1949 in Kenya wanting places for 40/10/1 per cent of African children at junior primary/senior primary/secondary). This partly concedes the 'agency' school's point; cite alongside the Kikuyu schools for Module 2 Mau Mau background. Uganda 1953 voted ~GBP 11m from the Cotton Price Stabilization Fund for welfare schemes

Mau Mau and schools (Module 2 Mau Mau lesson): Rodney says that when the war broke out the British closed 149 schools of the Kikuyu Independent Schools Association, 21 of the Kikuyu Karinga Education Association and 14 other Independent schools as 'training grounds for rebellion' (i.e. 184 schools in total: 149+21+14 = 184, checked). A strong education-and-land context for the Kenya lesson; verify the count against a Kenya specialist source (Anderson, Elkins) before using the exact figure [PROBABLE]

Typo/date: Rodney writes that Malagasy students organised the Vy Vato (VVS) society 'by 1816'; the Vy Vato Sakelika secret society dates from 1913 (the printed 1816 is a misprint for 1913 [check]). Do not repeat. Also in this chunk: Gold Coast 'crisis of primary-school leavers' and CPP youth as educated-but-frustrated (Nkrumah's CPP base was not 'illiterate'), Sudan Graduates' General Congress 1937 (100 schools in four years), Algeria's Association of Reformist Ulema schools (45,000 pupils by 1955), Felix Eboue's education push in FEA, Chief Essien of Calabar 1939 quote, Cabral's 'idiot boss' anecdote: use for the course's social-base-of-nationalism explanation (educated clerks and unemployed school-leavers)

Date error in Rodney: he places the French Brazzaville conference 'in 1948 (chaired by General de Gaulle)'; the Brazzaville Conference was held in 01-02/1944, and de Gaulle opened it; its final text ruled out self-government 'even in the distant future' (the quote he gives is accurate in substance). Use 1944. Other points: Guinea's 'no' vote in 1958 (French withdrawal) correct; Belgian professor (A. A. J. Van Bilsen) 1955 thirty-year plan for Congo independence (Rodney does not name him) ; Houphouet-Boigny quote 1948; Ghana, Sudan, Guinea early independence and Algeria/Kenya wars as 'domino' effect

Rodney on Pan-Africanism and independence causes (Module 3/4): Pan-African ideas forcefully expressed by West Indians and North Americans (Garvey, Padmore, Du Bois, Alpheus Hunton) because of slave-trade-era racial contradiction; independence caused by WWII, USSR, India/China, Indochina, Bandung 1955, Nasser, Ghana 1957, plus 'domino effect'; mass-party pressure ('boulders down a hillside') made British timetable collapse. Also trade-union strikes tied to independence in Gold Coast, Nigeria, Sudan; Sekou Toure's independent union; FEANF (Federation of Students of Black Africa). Says 'flag independence' was still a positive step (sovereignty regained), while most leaders were 'frankly capitalist'. He distinguishes a minority of non-capitalist leaders. Matches Module 4's multi-cause explanation

Babu's Postscript (12/1971) is the direct opposite of Moyo on every policy: foreign investment, exports for the 'world market', aid and loans are the cause not the solution of underdevelopment; 'vicious circle of poverty' theory rejected; he recommends delinking (examples: North Korea and Albania 'opted out of production for the world market') and attacks the Pearson Commission (Partners in Development, 1969) and the UN Second Development Decade (1% of GNP aid target). Outcomes since: North Korea suffered famine in the 1990s and Albania's isolation ended in 1991 collapse, so his two exemplars did not deliver; whereas export-led Asian economies (South Korea, Taiwan, China after 1978) grew fast: the central empirical test against Babu/Rodney, and the point where Moyo (who also cites East Asia) and mainstream economists disagree with them. Also says generals now 'the majority at the African summit' (1971), that Nyerere is Africa's only giant, and that Lumumba was murdered, Ben Bella and Nkrumah removed 'in response to the wishes of the imperialists' (contested attribution: Nkrumah's 1966 coup involved CIA interest per some accounts but is disputed [CONTESTED])
